books.section: Topic 5.9 Government Policies During the Civil War
Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley (August 22, 1862)

stimulus.source_note: Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862. Public domain. Wording verified against the Collected Works text. “. . .” marks omitted text between passages, quoted in their order in the source.
stimulus.text:
“My paramount object in this struggle is to save the Union, and is not either to save or to destroy slavery. . . . I have here stated my purpose according to my view of official duty; and I intend no modification of my oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.”

—Abraham Lincoln, letter to Horace Greeley, August 22, 1862

source: original; stimulus as noted in stimulus.source_note
stem: Lincoln distinguishes his “official duty” from his “personal wish that all men everywhere could be free.” That distinction best shows that Lincoln

options.text: put saving the Union ahead of his personal wish to free all men
believed his duty as president required him to destroy slavery at once
options.misconception: The letter says saving the Union is his paramount object, “not either to save or to destroy slavery” — destroying slavery at once was not his stated duty.

options.text: had no personal feelings about slavery one way or the other
options.misconception: Lincoln states his “oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free” — he had strong personal feelings about slavery.

options.text: would free enslaved people only in the loyal border states
options.misconception: Background from the books: the Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in rebel states and left the border states untouched — the opposite of this option.

rationales.A: Lincoln states his official purpose — saving the Union — and separately names his personal wish for universal freedom; the wish is personal, the duty is official, and the duty governs his actions.
rationales.B: The letter says saving the Union is his paramount object, “not either to save or to destroy slavery” — destroying slavery at once was not his stated duty.
rationales.C: Lincoln states his “oft-expressed personal wish that all men everywhere could be free” — he had strong personal feelings about slavery.
rationales.D: Background from the books: the Emancipation Proclamation freed enslaved people in rebel states and left the border states untouched — the opposite of this option.
rationales.general:
1. Lincoln draws a line between two things: what his office requires and what he personally wishes.
2. His office requires saving the Union; his wish is that all men everywhere could be free.
3. The letter's point is the order: the duty governs, and the wish does not override it.
4. Background from the books: a month later Lincoln issued the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation, defending emancipation as a war measure to save the Union.
Remember: a president's duty and his wishes are different things — the letter shows which one governed.
